{"id": "2:2/q01", "question": "What does 'that Book' refer to?", "turns_on": "The referent and whether distance is literal, retrospective, or inward.", "positions": [{"id": "2:2/q01/p1", "position": "The Qur’an, present or already known to its first hearers.", "reasons": "Early authorities gloss 'that' as 'this'; Khafāf's poem supports this usage. {"id": "2:2/q02", "question": "Why use dhālika and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "Whether distance is temporal, honorific, or literal, and the role of lām and kāf.", "positions": [{"id": "2:2/q02/p1", "position": "The form contains a demonstrative base, lām, and address kāf.", "reasons": "Basrans and Kufans dispute the base and lām's role: emphasis, distance, extra support or prevention of false annexation. {"id": "2:2/q03", "question": "What does kitāb signify here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word names a written product or asserts perfect bookhood.", "positions": [{"id": "2:2/q03/p1", "position": "Written and composed revelation, rooted in joining or gathering.", "reasons": "Poetic and Arabic examples include sewing, strung beads, assembled troops and joined letters. {"id": "2:2/q04", "question": "How is 'that Book' attached to the opening letters and what follows?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening letters are a name or completed utterance.", "positions": [{"id": "2:2/q04/p1", "position": "The letters, demonstrative, and Book admit subject, predicate, adjective and apposition analyses.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Rāzī and al-Samīn enumerate parses depending on whether the letters name a sūra, sound, or complete utterance. {"id": "2:2/q05", "question": "What do the opening letters contribute to 'that Book'?", "turns_on": "Whether their function is a marker, oath, challenge, or concealed secret.", "positions": [{"id": "2:2/q05/p1", "position": "They are an oath for the Qur’an, with the response supplied by 'that Book' or 'no doubt in it'.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba treats the letters as oath; Qāshānī says the answer is omitted and indicated by dhālika al-kitāb. {"id": "2:2/q07", "question": "What does 'no doubt in it' claim?", "turns_on": "Whether the statement describes the Book objectively, commands the hearer, or has a restricted audience.", "positions": [{"id": "2:2/q07/p1", "position": "The Book itself leaves no rational ground for doubt despite actual doubters.", "reasons": "The 2:23 challenge tests its miraculousness; al-Ṭabrisī denies obscurity and contradiction, and Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes doubts in hearers from defects in the Book. {"id": "2:2/q08", "question": "How does the negation work grammatically and rhetorically?", "turns_on": "The particle's scope, the function of fīhi, and whether word order suggests contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "2:2/q08/p1", "position": "Lā negates the genus, building rayb accusative without tanwīn.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares it to inna; Basran, Kufan and other accounts differ on government and omitted tanwīn. {"id": "2:21/q01", "question": "Why does the passage turn to a direct call?", "turns_on": "The sources give different explanations or scopes for the wording.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q01/p1", "position": "It rouses all the groups just described and makes the command vivid, serious, and easier to receive.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī call this iltifāt after believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites, comparing 1:5. {"id": "2:21/q03", "question": "How is ayyuhā al-nās constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether al-nās is the required nominative descriptor of a vocative ayy, an accusative by position, or part of a relative construction.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q03/p1", "position": "Ayy is a built vocative bridge to the definite al-nās; al-nās clarifies it in the nominative and hā adds attention.", "reasons": "Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Ṭabrisī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samin, and Ālūsī explain the bridge: direct yā plus al- would double definiteness; ambiguous ayy requires its descriptor, while hā reinforces the call or compensates for omitted annexation. Al-Khalīl's nominative rule and dialectal hā with ḍamma are reported. The Qurʾān repeats the layered call because weighty commands, warnings and promises demand attention."}, {"id": "2:21/q03/p2", "position": "The dependent noun may take the accusative by the vocative's underlying syntactic position.", "reasons": "Al-Māzinī and Abū ʿUthmān allow this by analogy with yā Zayd al-ẓarīf; Zajjāj, Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samin and Ālūsī object that actual Arab usage keeps this indispensable descriptor nominative."}, {"id": "2:21/q03/p3", "position": "Ayy is relative, with an omitted subject or clause, and al-nās completes that construction.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash gives the relative parse; Abū Ḥayyān records 'O those who are the people.' Samin favors direct address, while Ālūsī prefers the majority parse because it needs no deletion and avoids relative-clause restrictions."}, {"id": "2:21/q03/p4", "position": "The final vowel of al-nās is built rather than case inflection.", "reasons": "Abū Nizār says no governing ʿāmil accounts for its nominative; Manṣūr and Ibn al-Shajarī argue for inflection or analogy with the ordinary vocative ḍamma; Ālūsī finds these arguments weak."}, {"id": "2:21/q03/p5", "position": "The article on al-nās compensates for repeated vocative particles.", "reasons": "Abū Nizār proposes hā and al- in place of repeated yā; Ibn al-Shajarī rejects the imagined original yā ayy yā yā rajul and says the article can mark presence."}]}
{"id": "2:21/q04", "question": "What does al-nās mean as a word?", "turns_on": "The proposed root behind the name.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q04/p1", "position": "It denotes human beings as a species.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī lists insān as singular and nās and anāsī as plurals; other senses of related forms include sight, sound, knowledge and company. He records a doubled-s form for thirst, witnessed by a rajaz line, and the name al-nāsiya for water-scarce Mecca."}, {"id": "2:21/q04/p2", "position": "Its root points to human visibility or manifest presence.", "reasons": "Ibn Fāris connects ins with being visible."}, {"id": "2:21/q04/p3", "position": "Its name derives from movement toward aims.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī relates nās to naws, movement."}, {"id": "2:21/q04/p4", "position": "Its name derives from forgetfulness.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī records the proposed derivation of anas from human forgetfulness."}]}

asons": "Al-Suddī's report names these; Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports all polytheists, while noting that they know God as creator and provider despite general ignorance."}, {"id": "2:21/q05/p6", "position": "It addresses Jews specifically.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid are named by Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān."}]}

{"id": "2:21/q07", "question": "Does this general address include later people and the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether direct address reaches absent generations literally, by predominance, or by separate evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q07/p1", "position": "Later generations are bound through separate proof, although direct speech initially addresses those present.", "reasons": "Rāzī says absent people cannot hear a face-to-face command, but mass-transmitted evidence extends Muhammad's law. {"id": "2:21/q08", "question": "What does the command to worship require?", "turns_on": "Whether worship is specified as monotheism, obedience, or comprehensive servitude.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q08/p1", "position": "It calls for exclusive worship and affirmation of God's oneness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās repeatedly glosses worship as tawḥīd, and Baghawī reports every Qurʾānic instance thus. {"id": "2:21/q09", "question": "Does this command obligate unbelievers to perform religious duties?", "turns_on": "Whether the command covers subsidiary duties or only belief until conversion.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q09/p1", "position": "Unbelievers are also accountable for ritual duties, with belief as their prerequisite.", "reasons": "Rāzī says an imperative includes acquiring prerequisites, as water and purification; Bayḍāwī concurs. {"id": "2:21/q10", "question": "Can God command those who will not worship or cannot perform the act?", "turns_on": "Whether foreknowledge, motives, ability, and prerequisites make obligation impossible.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q10/p1", "position": "The command can bind even those known not to comply; it can include a prerequisite act of belief.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī uses 2:6 against a requirement for prior divine assistance. Rāzī answers that worship presupposes faith; his theological reply allows God as owner to impose even what others call impossible, while the general wording is qualified for children, insane, forgetful, unaware and incapable people (2:233). Ālūsī reports the same proof."}, {"id": "2:21/q10/p2", "position": "Such commands are impossible or purposeless.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports objections: unbelievers cannot recognize an unknown commander; equal motives paralyze choice, unequal motives force it; foreknowledge fixes acts; God cannot benefit and could confer benefits without burdens; divine creation of acts makes orders redundant; outward duties might obstruct inner knowledge. {"id": "2:21/q11", "question": "Why call God 'your Lord'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q11/p1", "position": "Lordship, nurture, mastery and prior favor make worship and gratitude due to Him.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī grounds duty in lordship; Abū Ḥayyān adds ownership and correction of servants' affairs. Harālī says rabb is more accessible through visible nurture than the divine name Allāh. Ālūsī distinguishes this immediate motive from perfected worship for God's essence. {"id": "2:21/q12", "question": "What does 'who created you' do in the description of Lord?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause praises the recognized Lord or distinguishes Him from alleged lords.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q12/p1", "position": "It praises God and gives the reason He deserves worship.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī, Wāḥidī, Bursevī, Biqāʿī and Ālūsī make the relative clause laudatory and causal; the creation and provision that follow establish divine oneness."}, {"id": "2:21/q12/p2", "position": "For polytheists, it identifies the true Lord against their supposed lords.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū Ḥayyān say the name rabb is shared in polytheist usage, while 'who created you' singles out God. {"id": "2:21/q13", "question": "How is alladhī khalaqakum parsed?", "turns_on": "The sources give different explanations or scopes for the wording.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q13/p1", "position": "Alladhī modifies rabbakum, and khalaqakum is its relative clause.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās takes kum as khalaqa's object; Samin also lists an accusative adjective parse."}, {"id": "2:21/q13/p2", "position": "Alladhī may instead be accusative or nominative by severance (qatʿ).", "reasons": "Samin lists both; Ibn al-Jazarī says an implied huwa or a commendatory accusative permits a good stop despite Sajawandī's objection."}]}
{"id": "2:21/q14", "question": "What does khalq mean?", "turns_on": "Whether it denotes divine origination, measured shaping, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q14/p1", "position": "It is bringing something into existence without a prior model.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī calls human measuring metaphorical; Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, Samin and Ālūsī retain origination as God's unique act. {"id": "2:21/q20", "question": "What variant readings are reported here?", "turns_on": "The transmitted forms and their grammatical analyses.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q20/p1", "position": "Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads wa-alladhīna man qablikum.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī takes the second relative as emphatic insertion, comparing Jarīr's doubled Taym; Abū Ḥayyān's grammarians object that emphasis should repeat its clause and reconstruct 'those who are before you.' {"id": "2:21/q21", "question": "What does laʿalla convey here?", "turns_on": "Whether the particle is purpose, human hope, a divine assurance, or an exhortation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q21/p1", "position": "It expresses hope or expectation from the human addressees' standpoint.", "reasons": "Sībawayh and others cite Moses and Aaron being told to speak gently in hope Pharaoh might remember (20:44), though God knew the outcome. {"id": "2:21/q22", "question": "To what does laʿallakum tattaqūn attach?", "turns_on": "Whether it qualifies the worship command or the act of creation, and whether a circumstantial parse is possible.", "positions": [{"id": "2:21/q22/p1", "position": "It attaches to 'created you': God created people with the means and prospect of piety.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya appeals to every child's fitra.
